title: The Positive and Negative Ways Leaders Apply Pressure
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece contrasts negative and positive forms of pressure that leaders apply as deadlines close in. Negative pressure treats everything as equally urgent, piles on fire drills and unrealistic expectations, and repeatedly signals disappointment -- tactics that erode trust and, paradoxically, urgency itself. Positive pressure instead pairs calm confidence with concrete support, explicit reasoning for why more speed is needed, and milestone checks that signal the moment deserves extra focus. The author closes with the line that turning every moment into a fire drill turns the team into firefighters instead of performers.
points: Negative pressure treats everything as urgent and offers no distinction between critical and routine work, which erodes both trust and urgency.
Positive pressure pairs urgency with visible support -- questions like 'What can I do to help?' rather than threats.
Adding milestone checks signals that a moment is genuinely different from routine work and deserves more focus.
Positive leaders explain the reasoning behind increased urgency and when the pressure will let up, rather than leaving it open-ended.
quotes: Negative pressure — urgency misapplied — can quickly erode performance and trust. In fact, when pressured negatively, team members often lose urgency.
Positive pressure is reflected by an attitude of calm and confidence. Good leaders own the urgency with the team, not with frenzy, but by showing up in support.
Because most other projects don’t include these milestone checks, adding them signals to the team that this moment is different and deserves more focus.
Positive leaders also go out of their way to explain why more urgency is needed without resorting to threats.
When leaders turn the moment into a fire drill, the team becomes firefighters, not performers.
